title: Modern and ML-Based Time Series Forecasting
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Modern and ML-Based Time Series Forecasting ##### 4,200 models, 11 hours, and one model that beat them all A retail chain in Hyderabad forecast weekly demand for 4,200 store-SKU combinations. Their pipeline fitted one SARIMA per series. It ran for 11 hours every Sunday night, failed on roughly 300 series with insufficient history, and needed a fallback rule for anything new. An engineer reframed it as a single supervised learning problem: one table with lag features, calendar features and store-item identifiers, and one LightGBM model trained across all series simultaneously. Training time: 4 minutes. MASE improved from 0.94 to 0.81. New store-SKU combinations worked immediately, because the model had learned patterns from similar items rather than needing history for that specific series. This is the **global model** advantage, and it is the biggest practical shift in forecasting over the last decade. Yesterday's classical methods model one series in isolation; today's approach treats forecasting as tabular supervised learning and lets the model borrow strength across series. ##### Reframing forecasting as supervised learning The core transformation: turn a sequence into a table where each row is one forecast target with features drawn from its past. ``` Original series: Supervised table: t y t lag1 lag2 lag7 roll7 dow month y 1 45 8 52 48 45 49.1 1 1 55 2 48 9 55 52 48 50.3 2 1 51 3 51 10 51 55 51 51.2 3 1 58 ... ... ``` ```python import numpy as np, pandas as pd def make_supervised(df: pd.DataFrame, target: str = "sales", id_cols: list[str] = ["store_id", "item_id"], ts_col: str = "date", horizon: int = 1) -> pd.DataFrame: """Build lag and rolling features. Every feature must use only the PAST.""" df = df.sort_values(id_cols + [ts_col]).copy() g = df.groupby(id_cols, observed=True)[target] # Lags — the direct signal. Start at `horizon` to respect the forecast gap. for lag in [horizon, horizon + 1, horizon + 2, 7, 14, 28, 52]: if lag >= horizon: df[f"lag_{lag}"] = g.shift(lag) # Rolling statistics on the LAGGED series — shift first, then roll shifted = g.shift(horizon) grouped = shifted.groupby([df[c] for c in id_cols], observed=True) for w in [4, 8, 13, 26, 52]: r = grouped.rolling(w, min_periods=max(2, w // 3)) df[f"roll{w}_mean"] = r.mean().reset_index(level=list(range(len(id_cols))), drop=True) df[f"roll{w}_std"] = r.std().reset_index(level=list(range(len(id_cols))), drop=True) df[f"roll{w}_max"] = r.max().reset_index(level=list(range(len(id_cols))), drop=True) # Trend and momentum df["momentum_4_13"] = df["roll4_mean"] / df["roll13_mean"].replace(0, np.nan) df["deviation"] = ((df[f"lag_{horizon}"] - df["roll13_mean"]) / df["roll13_std"].replace(0, np.nan)) # Expanding statistics — all history to date df["expanding_mean"] = (grouped.expanding() .mean().reset_index(level=list(range(len(id_cols))), drop=True)) # Calendar ts = df[ts_col] df["dow"] = ts.dt.dayofweek df["week"] = ts.dt.isocalendar().week.astype(int) df["month"] = ts.dt.month df["quarter"] = ts.dt.quarter df["is_month_end"] = ts.dt.is_month_end.astype("int8") df["week_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["week"] / 52) df["week_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["week"] / 52) df["month_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["month"] / 12) df["month_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["month"] / 12) # Time index — lets the model learn a global trend df["t"] = (ts - ts.min()).dt.days return df ``` Three details determine whether this works. **`shift(horizon)` before every rolling window.** Forecasting 4 weeks ahead means you will not know last week's value at prediction time — the shift must match the horizon, not default to 1. Getting this wrong produces a backtest that looks excellent and a production model that has no inputs. **Cyclical encoding** for week and month, so week 52 sits next to week 1 rather than 51 units away. **The `t` index** lets a tree model learn level shifts, though it cannot extrapolate a trend beyond the training range — which matters and is covered below. ##### Direct versus recursive multi-step Two strategies for forecasting more than one step ahead, with different failure modes. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Need h-step forecast] --> B{Strategy} B -->|Recursive| C[Train ONE model for 1 step] C --> D[Predict t+1, feed it back as a lag] D --> E[Predict t+2 using the prediction] E --> F[Errors COMPOUND across the horizon] B -->|Direct| G[Train h separate models,
one per horizon] G --> H[Each predicts its horizon independently] H --> I[No compounding, but h models to maintain] ``` ```python # Direct: one model per horizon, each with its own shift models = {} for h in range(1, 13): df_h = make_supervised(raw, horizon=h) train_h = df_h[df_h.date < cutoff].dropna(subset=feature_cols + ["sales"]) models[h] = lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=500, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=42, verbose=-1) models[h].fit(train_h[feature_cols], train_h["sales"]) # Recursive: one model, predictions fed back def recursive_forecast(model, history: pd.DataFrame, horizon: int) -> np.ndarray: preds = [] working = history.copy() for step in range(horizon): features = build_features_from(working) p = model.predict(features.tail(1))[0] preds.append(p) working = append_prediction(working, p) # the prediction becomes an input return np.array(preds) ``` | | Direct | Recursive | |---|---|---| | Models to train | h | 1 | | Error compounding | None | **Yes, grows with h** | | Long horizons | Better | Degrades | | Training cost | h× | 1× | | Consistency across horizons | Can be non-monotonic | Smooth | **Use direct for horizons beyond about 3–4 steps.** Recursive forecasting feeds predictions back as inputs, so a small error at step 1 becomes an input error at step 2, and by step 12 the model is reasoning about a trajectory it partly invented. A middle path, `mlforecast`, handles both cleanly: ```python from mlforecast import MLForecast from mlforecast.target_transforms import Differences import lightgbm as lgb fcst = MLForecast( models={"lgbm": lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=500, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=42, verbose=-1)}, freq="W", lags=[1, 2, 4, 8, 13, 26, 52], lag_transforms={ 1: [("rolling_mean", 4), ("rolling_mean", 13), ("rolling_std", 13)], 4: [("rolling_mean", 8)], }, date_features=["week", "month", "quarter"], target_transforms=[Differences([52])], # remove annual seasonality num_threads=8, ) fcst.fit(train_long, id_col="unique_id", time_col="ds", target_col="y") preds = fcst.predict(h=12) ``` ##### Prophet Facebook's Prophet decomposes a series into interpretable additive components: ``` y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε trend seasonality holidays ``` Its design goal was forecasting at scale by analysts rather than statisticians — sensible defaults, automatic changepoint detection, and native holiday handling. ```python from prophet import Prophet from prophet.diagnostics import cross_validation, performance_metrics df_prophet = train.rename(columns={"date": "ds", "sales": "y"}) m = Prophet( growth="linear", yearly_seasonality=True, weekly_seasonality=True, daily_seasonality=False, seasonality_mode="multiplicative", # when seasonal swing scales with level changepoint_prior_scale=0.05, # THE key parameter — trend flexibility seasonality_prior_scale=10.0, interval_width=0.80, ) # Indian festivals — Prophet handles moving holidays natively festivals = pd.DataFrame({ "holiday": "diwali", "ds": pd.to_datetime(["2023-11-12", "2024-11-01", "2025-10-20", "2026-11-08"]), "lower_window": -7, # effect starts a week before "upper_window": 3, }) m = Prophet(holidays=festivals, seasonality_mode="multiplicative") # Exogenous regressors m.add_regressor("is_promo", mode="multiplicative") m.add_regressor("price_index", mode="additive") m.fit(df_prophet) future = m.make_future_dataframe(periods=52, freq="W") future = future.merge(exog_future, on="ds", how="left") forecast = m.predict(future) m.plot(forecast) m.plot_components(forecast) # trend, seasonality and holiday effects separately ``` **`changepoint_prior_scale` is the parameter that matters most.** Too low and the trend is rigid, missing genuine level shifts; too high and it chases noise, producing wild extrapolations. Tune it by cross-validation: ```python from itertools import product param_grid = {"changepoint_prior_scale": [0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5], "seasonality_prior_scale": [0.1, 1.0, 10.0]} results = [] for cps, sps in product(*param_grid.values()): m = Prophet(changepoint_prior_scale=cps, seasonality_prior_scale=sps, seasonality_mode="multiplicative").fit(df_prophet) cv = cross_validation(m, initial="730 days", period="90 days", horizon="180 days", parallel="processes") results.append({"cps": cps, "sps": sps, "mae": performance_metrics(cv)["mae"].mean()}) print(pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values("mae").head()) ``` The honest assessment: **Prophet's strengths are interpretability, holiday handling and robustness to missing data.** Its component plots are genuinely useful for explaining a forecast to a stakeholder. Its accuracy is frequently mediocre against a tuned gradient boosting model, and it can extrapolate trends unrealistically far. Use it when explainability matters more than the last few points of accuracy, or as one member of an ensemble. ##### Gradient boosting for forecasting The workhorse of modern applied forecasting, and what won the Hyderabad comparison. ```python import lightgbm as lgb from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error feature_cols = [c for c in df.columns if c not in ["sales", "date", "store_id", "item_id"]] model = lgb.LGBMRegressor( objective="tweedie", # good for non-negative, zero-inflated demand tweedie_variance_power=1.2, n_estimators=3000, learning_rate=0.03, num_leaves=127, min_child_samples=50, subsample=0.8, subsample_freq=1, colsample_bytree=0.8, reg_lambda=1.0, random_state=42, verbose=-1, ) model.fit( train[feature_cols], train["sales"], eval_set=[(valid[feature_cols], valid["sales"])], eval_metric="mae", categorical_feature=["store_id", "item_id", "category"], callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(150, verbose=False)], ) ``` Three choices worth explaining. **`objective="tweedie"`** suits demand data that is non-negative with many zeros — a compound Poisson-gamma process, which is exactly what intermittent retail demand looks like. For continuous positive targets, `objective="poisson"` or a log-transformed target with MSE also work. **Categorical features declared natively**, so `store_id` and `item_id` become learnable entity embeddings rather than 4,200 one-hot columns. **The critical limitation: trees cannot extrapolate.** A tree predicts by averaging leaf values, and every leaf value comes from training data. If sales have grown steadily and you forecast beyond the observed range, the model predicts the highest value it has seen and no higher. Two standard fixes: ```python # Fix 1: detrend before modelling, add the trend back afterwards from scipy.stats import linregress def detrend(y: pd.Series): t = np.arange(len(y)) slope, intercept, *_ = linregress(t, y) return y - (slope * t + intercept), slope, intercept # Fix 2: model the difference or ratio instead of the level df["target_diff"] = df.groupby(["store_id", "item_id"])["sales"].diff(52) df["target_ratio"] = df["sales"] / df["lag_52"].replace(0, np.nan) ``` Modelling the year-over-year difference or ratio makes the target stationary, which removes the extrapolation problem entirely — the model predicts a change, and you add it to a known base. ##### Global models The Hyderabad transformation. Instead of one model per series, train a single model on all series with the series identity as a feature. ```python # Long format: every series stacked into one table long = df.melt(id_vars=["date"], var_name="series_id", value_name="y") long = make_supervised(long, id_cols=["series_id"]) # Series-level features let the model learn WHICH series it is looking at series_stats = long.groupby("series_id")["y"].agg( series_mean="mean", series_std="std", series_cv=lambda s: s.std() / s.mean(), series_zero_pct=lambda s: (s == 0).mean(), series_length="size", ).reset_index() long = long.merge(series_stats, on="series_id") # Normalise the target per series so scales are comparable long["y_scaled"] = long["y"] / long["series_mean"].replace(0, np.nan) global_model = lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=2000, learning_rate=0.03, num_leaves=255, random_state=42, verbose=-1) global_model.fit(long[feature_cols], long["y_scaled"], categorical_feature=["series_id", "category", "region"]) ``` **Target scaling is the detail that makes global models work.** Without it, a model trained on series ranging from 5 to 50,000 units spends its capacity learning scale rather than pattern. Dividing by each series' mean (or using a log transform) puts every series on a comparable footing. | | Local (one model per series) | Global (one model, all series) | |---|---|---| | Training time | O(n_series) | O(1) | | Short series | Fails or falls back | **Borrows from similar series** | | New series | No history, no model | Works from features immediately | | Series-specific quirks | Captured perfectly | May be smoothed away | | Cross-series patterns | Invisible | Learned | | Operational complexity | 4,200 artifacts to manage | One | **When global wins:** many related series, short individual histories, shared drivers (promotions, seasonality, weather), and new series appearing regularly. This describes most retail, most IoT, and most SaaS usage forecasting. **When global does not help:** a handful of long, genuinely unrelated series with different dynamics. Forecasting GDP, electricity demand and a single product's sales in one model is unlikely to beat three specialised models. The pragmatic answer is usually a **hybrid** — a global model for the bulk, with local models for a small number of high-value series that justify individual attention. ##### Deep learning for forecasting Worth knowing by name, and worth being sceptical about for tabular business forecasting. **LSTM/GRU** process sequences with a hidden state carrying information forward: ```python import torch, torch.nn as nn class LSTMForecaster(nn.Module): def __init__(self, n_features, hidden=64, layers=2, horizon=12, dropout=0.2): super().__init__() self.lstm = nn.LSTM(n_features, hidden, layers, batch_first=True, dropout=dropout if layers > 1 else 0) self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(hidden, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, horizon)) def forward(self, x): # x: (batch, seq_len, n_features) out, _ = self.lstm(x) return self.head(out[:, -1, :]) # use the final hidden state ``` **N-BEATS** stacks fully-connected blocks with backward and forward residual links, and was the first pure deep learning architecture to convincingly beat statistical methods on the M4 competition. **Temporal Fusion Transformer** adds attention and handles static, known-future and observed covariates explicitly, with interpretable attention weights. ```python from neuralforecast import NeuralForecast from neuralforecast.models import NBEATS, NHITS, TFT nf = NeuralForecast( models=[ NBEATS(h=12, input_size=52, max_steps=500, random_seed=42), NHITS(h=12, input_size=52, max_steps=500, random_seed=42), ], freq="W", ) nf.fit(df_long) preds = nf.predict() ``` The honest positioning: **deep learning forecasting needs a lot of data and a lot of tuning to beat well-engineered gradient boosting on tabular business series.** The M5 competition — 42,000 Walmart series — was won by LightGBM with careful feature engineering, not by a neural architecture. Deep models earn their place with very long sequences, high-frequency data, or genuinely complex multivariate dependencies. ##### Backtesting and comparison Everything must be evaluated the same way, and it must be rolling-origin. ```python from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error def backtest_ml(df, model_fn, feature_cols, target="sales", date_col="date", initial_days=730, horizon_days=84, step_days=84): """Rolling origin for a supervised forecasting model.""" dates = np.sort(df[date_col].unique()) origin = dates[0] + pd.Timedelta(days=initial_days) results = [] while origin + pd.Timedelta(days=horizon_days) <= dates[-1]: train = df[df[date_col] < origin] test = df[(df[date_col] >= origin) & (df[date_col] < origin + pd.Timedelta(days=horizon_days))] if len(test) == 0: break model = model_fn() model.fit(train[feature_cols], train[target]) pred = model.predict(test[feature_cols]) results.append({ "origin": origin, "mae": mean_absolute_error(test[target], pred), "mase": mean_absolute_error(test[target], pred) / naive_mae(train[target]), "n_test": len(test), }) origin += pd.Timedelta(days=step_days) return pd.DataFrame(results) comparison = [] for name, fn in [ ("seasonal_naive", lambda: SeasonalNaive(season=52)), ("ARIMA", lambda: SarimaxWrapper(order=(1,1,1), seasonal_order=(1,1,1,52))), ("Prophet", lambda: ProphetWrapper(seasonality_mode="multiplicative")), ("LightGBM local", lambda: lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=500, verbose=-1)), ("LightGBM global", lambda: GlobalLGBM(n_estimators=2000)), ]: bt = backtest_ml(df, fn, feature_cols) comparison.append({"model": name, "mae": bt.mae.mean(), "mase": bt.mase.mean(), "mase_std": bt.mase.std()}) print(pd.DataFrame(comparison).sort_values("mase").round(4)) ``` **Report MASE with its standard deviation across folds.** A model with MASE 0.81 ± 0.04 is meaningfully better than one at 0.79 ± 0.22 — the second is unstable and will occasionally produce a forecast much worse than naive. And the practical finding from every forecasting competition: **simple ensembles beat individual models.** ```python ensemble = (0.4 * preds_lgbm + 0.3 * preds_prophet + 0.3 * preds_arima) ``` Averaging forecasts from methods with different inductive biases reduces variance in the same way ensembling reduces variance anywhere. A median across three methods is robust and takes one line. ##### Common mistakes - Rolling features without shifting by the forecast horizon. - Recursive multi-step at long horizons, compounding errors. - Tree models forecasting beyond the training range without detrending. - No target scaling in a global model, so capacity goes to learning scale. - Random train/test splits. - Prophet's `changepoint_prior_scale` left at default on a series with structural breaks. - Deep learning on 200 series with 80 observations each. - Comparing methods on different backtest protocols. - Reporting MASE without its variability across folds. - No baseline, so it is unknown whether any of it helped. ##### Hands-on Reframe a forecasting task as supervised learning with lag and calendar features, being careful that every feature is shifted by the forecast horizon. Train a gradient boosting forecaster and compare it via rolling-origin backtesting against Prophet and your earlier ARIMA model, all on identical folds. Then deliberately break the shift — use `shift(1)` for a 4-step horizon — and observe how much the backtest inflates. That gap is the most instructive number in the exercise. For the mini-project, build a global forecasting model across many related series using engineered features and gradient boosting. Include target scaling per series, series-level features, native categorical handling for series identity, and a detrending or differencing step so the model can handle growth. Backtest against per-series ARIMA and seasonal naive baselines, and produce a report on **when the global approach wins** — segment the results by series length, volume and volatility, because the global advantage is largest on short, low-volume series and can disappear on long, high-volume ones. Include a simple ensemble and report whether it beats every individual member. For the assignment, explain the advantage of a single global model over fitting one model per series, and when it might not help. Cover the borrowing-strength mechanism, the operational simplification, and the specific conditions — few series, long histories, unrelated dynamics — under which local models remain the right choice. ##### Key takeaways - Reframing forecasting as supervised learning unlocks gradient boosting, but every feature must be shifted by the forecast horizon. - Use direct multi-step beyond about four steps; recursive forecasting compounds its own errors. - Trees cannot extrapolate — detrend, difference, or model a ratio when the series is growing. - Global models borrow strength across series, handle new series immediately, and need per-series target scaling to work. - Backtest everything on identical rolling-origin folds, report MASE with its variability, and try a simple ensemble.
